::: {.kw-overview}
Donor utilisation is the spine of this issue. An OPTN analysis records the moment donation after circulatory death stopped being the marginal pathway and became the majority one — half of all US kidney donors by the middle of this year — while simultaneously showing that a third of the DCD kidneys recovered are now discarded, and an Australasian registry study of ten thousand recipients supplies the long-term reassurance that the expansion rests on, with graft survival and ten-year function matching donation after brain death despite double the delayed graft function and a clear excess of early rejection. Preservation follows naturally: perfusate complement measurements taken during prolonged normothermic machine perfusion in a UK phase 1 trial predicted which kidneys would develop functional delayed graft function and added information beyond the UK donor risk index, which is the first credible route to using the perfusion circuit as an assessment platform rather than merely a storage one. Two papers then reopen the question of how we monitor immunosuppression, and specifically tacrolimus, a drug whose pharmacology we still measure in a way that has changed little in thirty years: a post hoc analysis of the ALLEGRO trial argues that plasma rather than whole blood concentration is what tracks nephrotoxicity, and a Wisconsin cohort of nearly two thousand recipients shows that variability between troughs beyond the first year carries more prognostic weight than the trough itself. The issue closes on three papers about who gets a transplant and how we predict what happens next — a multicentre validation showing the iBox prognostication system performs equivalently in African American recipients, a 29,874-transplant registry analysis rehabilitating right-sided minimally invasive living donor nephrectomy provided the procurement technique is right, and a seventeen-year Australian cohort locating sex inequity in access squarely in the referral and evaluation pathway rather than in allocation.
:::

---

### 1. [Temporal Changes in the Recovery and Utilization of Kidneys Donated After Circulatory Death in the United States](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.09.014)
[Husain SA, Zeiser L, Ishaque T, Orandi BJ, Levan ML, Stern JM, Motter JD, Lonze BE, Coons BE, Lipton MK, Sommer PM, Bae S, Parent B, Segev DL, Massie AB, Stewart DE. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42722333.]{.kw-ref}

Kidneys from donation after circulatory death donors were historically recovered and used less often than those from brain-dead donors, and this OPTN analysis documents how completely that has inverted in the United States over a decade. Comparing three eras — 2016–2019, 2020–2022 and 2023–2025 — the proportion of kidney donors who were DCD rose from 21.0% to 30.6% and then to 42.4%, and by the second quarter of 2025 more than half of all kidney donors, 50.4%, were DCD. The composition of the DCD donor pool changed alongside the volume: kidneys transplanted in the most recent era were more likely to come from donors over 60 or with diabetes, hypertension or obesity, and more likely to come from donors who died of cardiovascular disease or stroke, with 86.8% of them pumped. The uncomfortable counterpart is discard, which rose in step — the non-use rate among recovered DCD kidneys climbed from 20.8% in the first era to 29.9% and then 35.4%, with the donors whose kidneys went unused in the latest era carrying more comorbidities than in earlier eras. Variation between organisations remained extreme throughout, with the DCD share ranging from 0% to 38% across recovering organ procurement organisations in the first era and from 0.4% to 60% in the third, and a comparably wide spread across transplanting centres. The authors' conclusion is that with half of kidney donors now following the DCD pathway, the priority shifts from expanding recovery to refining donor selection and management so that recovered organs are actually used. UK practice reached majority-DCD earlier and has a national retrieval service that constrains exactly the inter-centre variation this paper documents, so the value here is less as a warning than as a natural experiment — it shows what happens to discard rates when DCD expansion outpaces the assessment tools needed to decide which of those kidneys are transplantable.

### 2. [Kidney Donation After Circulatory Death Is Associated With Sustained Graft Function, Comparable Graft, and Patient Survival](https://doi.org/10.1097/TXD.0000000000001997)
[Xu AL, Kholmurodova F, Irish GL, Clayton PA. *Transplant Direct*, 2026. PMID: 42725169.]{.kw-ref}

If the OPTN paper describes how far DCD expansion has gone, this ANZDATA analysis asks whether the long-term outcome data justify it, and extends the follow-up on graft function further than previous work. The authors included all 10,144 adults who received a deceased donor kidney-only transplant in Australia or New Zealand between January 2010 and December 2023, of whom 2,738 (26.9%) received a kidney from a donor after circulatory determination of death, excluding paediatric, multi-organ and out-of-region recipients, and adjusted their models using a kidney donor risk index modified to remove the DCD component so that donor type was not counted twice. Graft survival censored for death was indistinguishable between the two pathways (adjusted hazard ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.94–1.24, p = 0.27), and survival of the patients themselves came out nominally better in the circulatory-death group (aHR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37–0.89, p = 0.01) — a finding the authors themselves decline to treat as real, pointing to five-year survival of 87.9% against 88.3% and ten-year survival of 73.9% against 70.1% and noting there is no plausible mechanism by which the circulatory-death pathway would confer a survival advantage. Graft function is the novel contribution: mean eGFR at one month was 42 mL/min/1.73 m² in DCD recipients against 53 in brain-death recipients, but the DCD curve rose significantly more steeply (p < 0.001 for both spline interaction terms), converged by five years and stayed converged out to ten. The early cost was substantial, with delayed graft function in 55.0% of DCD recipients against 24.1%, and rejection within twelve months in 20.9% against 16.5% (odds ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.20–1.53), driven more by antibody-mediated (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.34–2.17) than cellular rejection (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.06–1.47). The authors are candid that registry selection bias cannot be excluded and that ANZDATA captures no machine perfusion data at all, which matters because they explicitly flag that their cohort achieved these results with limited perfusion use and no normothermic regional perfusion anywhere in the region. For UK units that is the most interesting sentence in the paper: it implies that the long-term parity British practice already relies on was demonstrated here without the preservation technology the UK routinely deploys, and that the early rejection excess — not late graft loss — is where the remaining DCD penalty actually sits.

### 3. [Characterising Prognostic Complement Biomarkers During Clinical Normothermic Machine Perfusion for Renal Transplantation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2026.09.003)
[Fallon J, Dumbill R, Knight S, Ploeg R, Friend P, van Kooten C, Hunter J. *Am J Transplant*, 2026. PMID: 42705465.]{.kw-ref}

Normothermic machine perfusion is usually justified as a way of reconditioning a kidney, but its more valuable property may be that it creates a window in which the organ can be interrogated before the decision to implant — and complement activation, which is central to ischaemia-reperfusion injury, has not previously been characterised during clinical kidney NMP. Drawing samples and outcome data from NKP1, a phase 1 trial in which 36 kidneys underwent prolonged NMP before being implanted, the authors assayed eight perfusate analytes at hour 1 and again at the end of perfusion, spanning the classical and lectin pathways (C1s, collectin-11, C2), the alternative pathway (factor B, Ba), central C3 and its activation fragment C3d, and the terminal soluble C5b-9 complex. The complement cascade was demonstrably active during perfusion: C1s, collectin-11, C3d and soluble C5b-9 all rose across the perfusion period while C2 and factor B fell, a consumption-and-generation pattern consistent with genuine activation rather than assay drift. Kidneys that went on to develop functional delayed graft function had higher soluble C5b-9 at end perfusion and higher C3 at hour 1, both of which survived false discovery rate correction. Complement profiles also stratified time to a 50% fall in serum creatinine, and did so within strata of the UK donor risk index, with an hour-1 grouping improving Cox model fit beyond UKDRI alone — meaning the perfusate signal is adding information the standard UK donor risk tool does not already contain. Paired biopsies taken before perfusion and after reperfusion showed increased tissue C5b-9 and ICAM-1 but no increase in C4d, locating the injury in terminal pathway activation and endothelial activation rather than in classical antibody-driven complement fixation. Thirty-six kidneys is a phase 1 sample and these are associations, not a validated assay, but the authors' framing — biomarker-guided assessment and, in time, targeted complement intervention during perfusion — is the right one. For UK practice this is the most directly transferable paper in this issue: it uses a UK trial cohort, benchmarks against the UKDRI that British units already apply, and points towards the version of machine perfusion that would actually change acceptance decisions rather than just improving storage.

### 4. [Plasma versus Whole Blood Tacrolimus Concentration and Outcomes After Kidney Transplantation: Post Hoc Analysis of the ALLEGRO Trial](https://doi.org/10.2215/CJN.0000001214)
[Jonker J, van den Born JC, Kremer D, van Sandwijk MS, Gelinck A, Meziyerh S, Moes DJAR, Smit C, Gomes-Neto AW, Hilhorst M, Vart P, Berger SP, Bakker SJL, Florquin S, de Vries APJ, Bemelman FJ, Touw DJ, Sanders JSF. *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42726515.]{.kw-ref}

Every transplant unit doses tacrolimus against a whole blood trough, and the awkward fact underlying that practice is that most of what the assay measures is bound to erythrocytes and pharmacologically inactive — so this post hoc analysis of the ALLEGRO trial asks whether the plasma concentration, which should better reflect the free active fraction, tracks outcomes more faithfully. The parent trial had allocated 295 kidney transplant recipients across three arms — conventional triple therapy, a reduced-exposure tacrolimus arm, and an arm in which prednisolone was stopped; for this analysis plasma concentrations were assayed by LC-MS/MS, related to eGFR by linear regression, compared against the whole blood measure by bootstrap resampling, related to biopsy findings by logistic regression and to infection by joint modelling. Mean recipient age was 56.5 ± 13.2 years and 95 (32%) were female. Over the first post-transplant month, a higher mean plasma level (0.31 ± 0.17 ng/mL) tracked worse function at four weeks (standardised β −0.17, 95% CI −0.29 to −0.05, P = 0.006) while the whole blood level showed nothing (β 0.09, −0.03 to 0.22, P = 0.15), and the gap between those two associations was itself statistically significant (P = 0.004). Later exposure behaved identically: averaged across 6.5 to 24 months, the plasma level (0.15 ± 0.07 ng/mL) predicted lower eGFR at two years (β −0.19, −0.35 to −0.03, P = 0.02) where the whole blood level did not (β 0.04, −0.13 to 0.20, P = 0.66), the two again differing significantly (P = 0.02). Histology pointed the same way, with moderate-to-severe arteriolar hyalinosis in 10 (14%) of 71 two-year protocol biopsies and late plasma concentration associated with that lesion (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.07–3.80, P = 0.03) where whole blood concentration was not (OR 1.65, 0.83–3.53, P = 0.17). Neither measure predicted infection, and neither predicted rejection — though with only 22 biopsy-proven rejection episodes (7%) the trial is underpowered to detect the efficacy side of the ledger, which is precisely the half a UK unit would need before changing an assay. The honest reading, which the authors share, is that plasma concentration looks like the better marker of calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity and not yet like a better marker of anything else; larger studies are needed, and no British laboratory should be reconfiguring therapeutic drug monitoring on this evidence.

### 5. [Monitoring Long-term Tacrolimus Exposure: Metrics, Trajectories, and Associations with Outcomes after Kidney Transplantation in the Wisconsin Allograft Recipient Database (WisARD)](https://doi.org/10.1159/000552040)
[Yuan Z, Parajuli S, Mandelbrot D, Astor BC. *Am J Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42684985.]{.kw-ref}

Where the ALLEGRO analysis asks what to measure, this Wisconsin cohort asks how to summarise what we already measure once a recipient is years out from transplantation, a period in which there is no consensus on the right monitoring metric and surprisingly little data on how exposure drifts. The authors examined tacrolimus exposure beyond the first post-transplant year in 1,994 recipients on tacrolimus-based immunosuppression who survived at least twelve months with a functioning graft, comparing five candidate metrics — the mean trough, intra-patient variability, and the proportions of time spent within, below and above the therapeutic range — against four endpoints: rejection occurring late, graft failure both with and without censoring for death, and death in a patient whose graft was still working. Over a median 5.3 years of follow-up, exposure declined steadily, which is the expected clinical drift but is rarely quantified. The metric that mattered was not the average but the scatter: high intra-patient variability, defined as a coefficient of variation of 30% or more, measured during the second post-transplant year showed the strongest association with outcome, raising the risk of graft failure by 45% on the uncensored analysis (adjusted hazard ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.22–1.72, p < 0.01). High variability was also associated with death-censored graft failure, with mortality and with late rejection, and cumulative high variability across the preceding five years likewise predicted graft failure and death — so the signal is not confined to a single vulnerable year. This is a single-centre database study without randomisation, so variability may be as much a marker of adherence, absorption and comorbidity as a causal exposure, and the paper cannot tell a clinician that reducing variability improves outcomes. It does, however, make an operationally cheap argument for UK units: the trough values needed to compute a coefficient of variation are already sitting in every recipient's record, and flagging the patients whose second-year variability exceeds 30% identifies a group at materially higher risk of losing the graft without requiring a single additional test.

### 6. [Performance of the iBox Prognostication System in African American Kidney Transplant Recipients](https://doi.org/10.1681/ASN.0000001247)
[Truchot A, Lombardi Y, Raynaud M, Aubert O, Divard G, Thalamas T, Astor B, Mandelbrot D, Parajuli S, Newell KA, Larsen CP, Karadkhele G, Orandi B, Friedewald JJ, Gupta G, Akalin E, Jordan SC, Matas AJ, Molnar MZ, Yamauchi J, Fornadi K, Bentall AJ, Stegall MD, Mannon RB, Segev DL, Huang E, Fitzsimmons WE, Loupy A. *J Am Soc Nephrol*, 2026. PMID: 42720987.]{.kw-ref}

Prediction models that perform well overall can fail badly in subgroups, and for a tool like iBox — increasingly used as a surrogate endpoint in trials as well as a clinical prognostic aid — that possibility is not academic, since African American recipients experience worse long-term graft outcomes and were not separately examined when the model was developed. This multicentre North American study assessed 3,866 kidney transplant recipients, 1,040 of them — 27% of the cohort — identified as African American, testing discrimination, calibration, overall fit and clinical utility both across the whole group and within each subgroup. Discrimination was essentially equivalent, with a c-index of 0.80 (95% CI 0.77–0.83) in African American recipients against 0.83 (0.81–0.85) in non-African American recipients, a difference that did not reach significance (p = 0.07). Calibration was likewise similar, with observed-to-expected graft loss ratios of 1.08 (0.95–1.23) and 0.99 (0.88–1.10) respectively (p = 0.28), and no significant interaction between iBox score and race in multivariable analysis stratified by transplant centre (p = 0.29). The findings held whichever of the three filtration-rate equations was fed into the model — the kidney recipient specific formula, CKD-EPI or MDRD — with only minor calibration differences between them, which is reassuring at a moment when eGFR equations are themselves being revised for race-free reporting. Performance was sustained up to seven years from the point of risk evaluation. The slightly lower point estimate for discrimination in African American recipients is worth holding lightly rather than dismissing, since a study of this size can exclude a large subgroup failure but not a modest one. For UK units the direct relevance is limited — this is a North American cohort using a US racial classification that maps poorly onto British populations — but the methodological point travels: iBox is being adopted here as a trial endpoint and a counselling tool, and subgroup validation of the kind done here is what should precede that adoption in any given population, including the ethnic groups that dominate UK transplant waiting lists.

### 7. [Safety of Right-Sided Minimally Invasive Living Donor Nephrectomy: A Contemporary National Registry Analysis of 29,874 Transplants](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.urology.2026.08.032)
[Gondolesi I, Jaber Di Tommaso S, Florman SS, Palese MA. *Urology*, 2026. PMID: 42674198.]{.kw-ref}

The reluctance to take the right kidney from a living donor rests on a short renal vein, a perceived thrombosis risk and a body of evidence largely predating contemporary minimally invasive technique — and this UNOS analysis of 29,874 living donor kidney transplants performed between 2021 and 2025 suggests the risk is real but attributable to how the kidney is retrieved rather than to which side it comes from. Right-sided minimally invasive donor nephrectomy was associated with longer cold ischaemia time (median 1.9 hours, IQR 1.1–4.4, against 1.6 hours, IQR 1.0–3.8; P < .001) and with roughly double the rate of delayed graft function (4.7% against 2.5%; P < .001). Across the cohort as a whole, right-sided kidneys also showed higher rates of graft thrombosis and early graft loss and lower four-year graft survival on Kaplan-Meier and Cox analysis. The critical finding is that none of that excess risk survived stratification by how the kidney was retrieved: it disappeared entirely among cases done without hand assistance, which places the hazard in the retrieval technique rather than in the laterality itself. Donor and recipient creatinine at last follow-up were clinically comparable, so whatever happens in the early period does not appear to leave a functional residue in the surviving grafts. Two caveats limit how far this can be pushed: registry follow-up is short for a graft survival endpoint, and the authors combined pure laparoscopic and robotic cases into a single non-hand-assisted category, so the analysis cannot say which of those two techniques is doing the work. Their conclusion is that taking the right kidney stays defensible where the unit is experienced and works laparoscopically without hand assistance, and for UK units — where laparoscopic donor nephrectomy is standard and hand-assisted technique is not universal — the practical implication is that a donor whose anatomy favours leaving the left kidney behind need not be declined on laterality grounds, provided the unit's own retrieval technique matches the one that performed well here.

### 8. [Sex and Intersectional Disparities in Access to Deceased Donor Kidney Transplantation: A 17-Year Population-Based Cohort Study](https://doi.org/10.1111/nep.70276)
[Vitagliano TL, De La Mata NL, Hsu PS, Alexander SI, Wyburn K, Wyld MLR. *Nephrology (Carlton)*, 2026. PMID: 42693385.]{.kw-ref}

That women are less likely to be waitlisted for a kidney transplant is one of the better-replicated findings in transplant epidemiology; what this Australian cohort adds is a precise answer to where in the pathway the disadvantage occurs and which women carry most of it. Using ANZDATA, the authors followed 47,884 adults and children who started dialysis in Australia between June 2006 and December 2023, contributing 147,510 person-years, excluding pre-emptive and multi-organ transplants; by study end 23% had been waitlisted and 47% had died without ever reaching the list. Female sex was associated with a 7% lower crude likelihood of waitlisting (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.89–0.97), and — revealingly — the gap widened rather than narrowed on adjustment, to 19% (aHR 0.81, 95% CI 0.77–0.84), because women in the cohort were on average clinically healthier than men. Interaction testing at a deliberately stringent threshold found significant effect modification by ethnicity, comorbidity burden, cause of kidney failure and BMI but not by age or socioeconomic position, and the subgroup estimates are stark: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women were 43% less likely to be waitlisted than their male peers (aHR 0.57, 95% CI 0.49–0.66), women with diabetic kidney disease 39% less likely (aHR 0.61, 0.56–0.67), women with obesity 31% less likely (aHR 0.69, 0.65–0.75), and the comorbidity gradient ran in an orderly dose-response from 13% among those with no comorbidities (aHR 0.87, 0.83–0.92) to 34% among those with three or more (aHR 0.66, 0.56–0.79). Once on the list the disparity vanished — deceased donor transplantation aHR 1.04 (0.99–1.10) and waitlist mortality aHR 0.91 (0.76–1.08) — which locates the inequity unambiguously in referral, evaluation and listing rather than in an allocation algorithm that is sex-blind by construction. The authors read the whole pattern as an implicit threshold applied more stringently to women, and support it with the observation that waitlisted women survived a median 4.52 years before dying on the list against 3.40 years for men, implying they were healthier when listed; they are appropriately clear that ANZDATA records sex and gender in a single clinician-entered variable, captures no referral milestones, and cannot exclude residual confounding by health literacy, caregiving burden or patient preference. The health system differs from the UK's, but the mechanism does not depend on financing — the authors note the same disparity across publicly funded systems in France, Germany, Austria and Canada — and the actionable inference for a UK unit is that auditing waitlisting rates alone will miss this, because the decisions that produce it happen before a patient is ever discussed for listing.
